Population Stability Index (PSI)

Source: R/dfr_psi.R
psi.Rd

Compares the distribution of a new sample with a baseline sample, feature by feature, through the Population Stability Index, the symmetrised Kullback-Leibler divergence of their binned distributions (Kurian and Allali, 2024): $$PSI = \sum_{i=1}^{B} (P_i - Q_i) \ln(P_i / Q_i),$$ where \(Q_i\) and \(P_i\) are the shares of the baseline and of the new sample in bin \(i\). The bins are quantile groups of the baseline (deciles for bins = 10, demi-deciles for bins = 20).

Usage

psi(expected, actual, bins = 10, thresholds = c(0.1, 0.25))

Arguments

expected

The baseline sample: a numeric vector, or a data frame or matrix with one column per feature.

actual

The new sample, with the same features as expected.

bins

Number of quantile groups of the baseline.

thresholds

Limits between the drift levels: PSI below the first is "little" drift, between the two "moderate" drift (to be reviewed), and above the second "significant" drift.

Value

A psi object: a list with summary, a data frame with one row per feature (feature, psi, level, number of bins), and bins, a data frame with one row per feature and bin (feature, bin, lower and upper baseline values, expected and actual shares, part, the contribution of the bin).

Details

The computation follows the SAS macro of the reference code (https://github.com/FrancisKurian/Kullback, PSI_computation.sas):

  1. The baseline is ranked (ties get their mean rank) and split into bins groups as PROC RANK GROUPS=: group floor(rank * bins / (n + 1)). Tied values always share a group, so heavily tied data may give fewer bins. Bin i covers the baseline values from its smallest to its largest.

  2. New values below the smallest baseline value or above the largest are moved to it (they fall in the first or the last bin).

  3. The shares are the bin counts over the sample sizes. Missing new values count in the size of the new sample but in no bin, so a stream that starts sending missing values lowers every share. Missing baseline values are left out. A new sample whose values are all missing has every share 0, and so a PSI of 0 (step 4): missing data must be checked separately.

  4. A bin without new values contributes 0, as in the reference (where the logarithm of 0 is missing and the missing part is set to 0).

The reference assigns a value through a SAS format built from the bin ranges; a new value that falls strictly between the largest value of a bin and the smallest of the next one matches no range and is dropped from the counts (but kept in the sample size). Here such a value goes to the lower bin. The paper's thresholds are 0.1 and 0.25 (Section 5; Section 3.1 uses 0.2 for the second). The PSI of two samples from the same distribution is not 0: it is about (bins - 1) (1 / n_expected + 1 / n_actual), which matters for small samples.

References

Kurian, J. F. and Allali, M. (2024). Detecting drifts in data streams using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure for data engineering applications. Journal of Data, Information and Management, 6, 207-216. doi:10.1007/s42488-024-00119-y

See also

dfr_psi() to monitor a stream, and dfr_kldist() for the same divergence over a sliding window with equal-width bins.

Examples

set.seed(1)
base <- stats::rnorm(10000, 610, 50)
new <- base
top <- new > 643 & stats::runif(10000) < 0.5
new[top] <- new[top] - 200
result <- psi(base, new)
result$summary
#>   feature       psi    level bins
#> 1   value 0.1858564 moderate   10
head(result$bins)
#>   feature bin    lower    upper expected actual         part
#> 1   value   1 426.4350 544.6399      0.1 0.2286 1.063269e-01
#> 2   value   2 544.6916 567.6745      0.1 0.1010 9.950331e-06
#> 3   value   3 567.7063 583.5134      0.1 0.1000 0.000000e+00
#> 4   value   4 583.5145 596.8759      0.1 0.1001 9.995003e-08
#> 5   value   5 596.9027 609.1905      0.1 0.1001 9.995003e-08
#> 6   value   6 609.2166 621.9483      0.1 0.1000 0.000000e+00
psi(base, new, bins = 20)$summary
#>   feature       psi    level bins
#> 1   value 0.2461855 moderate   20
